newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch biotech pioneer gears up to go public.
newsitem.headline: Dutch biotech pioneer gears up to go public.

text.p: For Dutch biopharmaceutical firm Pharming, the international furore unleashed by the recent cloning of Dolly the sheep in Britain sparks a strong sense of deja vu.

Researchers at Pharming pioneered the creation of Herman, the transgenic bull, in 1988, hitting the headlines in a blaze of media soul-searching about the morality of implanting human genes in animals.

While the rest of the world wrangles over the pros and cons of bio-engineering, Pharming has been quietly getting on with the business of modifying animals genetically to produce medicines from their milk, targeting what could prove to be a highly lucrative market.

"The debate raging now in Britain, the United States and elsewhere on the morality of bio-engineering started in the Netherlands about nine years ago," Pharming's corporate communications director Rob Meines said.
Genetically modified foodstuffs remain controversial but public acceptance of animal biotechnology to create more effective medicines for humans has since become widespread.
Pharming is within a couple of years of launching human lactoferrin derived from cows' milk -- a product that boosts the immune system and could become the company's biggest money-maker.
The product, used in the treatment and prevention of stomach infections, is expected to be introduced in association with food and dietary aids group Nutricia around the year 2000.
A second product to combat Pompey's disease, an incurable hereditary muscle-wasting illness, could be available by 1999.
Armed with these upbeat prospects for future performance, Pharming is looking to go public after years of government grants, venture capital funding and private stock placements.
"We plan to seek a stock market listing some time over the next year or so, but we're in no particular hurry as we have sufficient capital," says Pharming Chief Executive Officer George Hersbach.

Around 60 million guilders ($31 million) worth of Pharming shares are currently placed with some 50 to 60 different shareholders around the world, while the company is valued at an estimated 160 million guilders ($84 million).
Given this international spread, Pharming is mulling a dual listing on Nasdaq and the London Stock Exchange, while Easdaq, Nasdaq's recently created European equivalent, is also a possibility.

Pharming currently owns the rights to all pharmaceuticals production based on milk from genetically modified mammals in the United States, Europe, Canada, Russia, Australia and New Zealand. More patents are pending.
In the Netherlands, as elsewhere, the future looks bright for bio-engineering. Recent advances have made it one of the most effective and cost-efficient technologies in making drugs.
According to a recent government report, bio-engineered products will account for about 40 percent of Dutch pharmaceuticals sales in 2010 vs. 10 percent to 15 percent now.
"Pharming already has around 35 new projects targeted, of which two are already in the pipeline," Hersbach says. "It's a fast-growing industry."

The nascent boom in biotechnology prompts comparisons with the computer software sector and some analysts predict that bio-techs will take over from high-techs as the preferred choice of smart investors not averse to taking risks.
But with product development times averaging 10-12 years, it's not a sector for those looking to get rich quick.
"After nine years we are now into the final research phase for production of human lactoferrin in cow's milk, and that is relatively fast for the development of this type of product," Hersbach said.
The final phase involves trials on human subjects. "We hope to start trials with the first human adult patients around June this year," he said.
Human lactoferrin is a protein found in the milk of breast-feeding mothers that promotes infant immunity to bacterial infections and stimulates the growth of benign intestinal flora.

The bio-engineered product will be used for treating or preventing bacterial gastro-intestinal infections in patients with reduced immunological resistance, such as AIDS patients or cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy.
"Another application is in clinical formulas for premature babies," said Hersbach.
